prize_parts.citation: for credibly identified empirical analysis of how import competition and technological change reshape labour demand, wages and local labour-market adjustment

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed from B045 (Persson, Tabellini, Besley) to B037 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson. The change rests on the reasons I gave in round 1, not on the number of members who prefer B037. I ranked B037 sixth because it looked like a composite: the skill-premium and task strand and the import-shock strand have different originators, and the skill-premium strand sits next to ground the Academy recognised in 2023 and 2024. The Dorn variant, tied to a narrow citation, answers both objections. Autor, Dorn and Hanson are the identifiable authors of one coherent body of work, the local-labour-market evidence on import competition. It rests on transparent designs and hand-assembled regional data, and it tests a clear prediction: adjustment to a trade shock is slow, uneven and persistent. This is the standard I apply in my own field, where I trust results that confront theory with real data under a credible design. The central papers are now over a decade old. The finding has been replicated and qualified with data from other countries, and the debate is over magnitudes and persistence, not over whether the effect exists. The lesson is general and matters well beyond labour economics for how societies think about the costs of trade and technology. Autor's task and polarisation work can be credited through his name without adding a fourth or fifth author. The citation does not claim the task framework for the three laureates. I regard B045 and B025 as serious alternatives that I would not rule out. The two points that pushed me from B045 were the unresolved adjacency to the 2024 prize and the weaker identification of the cross-country constitutional evidence, which Fredriksson, Hassler and I all acknowledged and which I could not dispose of in round 1.
statement.case_against: The narrow citation costs something. It leaves out Katz and the long-run education-versus-technology framing that gives the trade evidence its general meaning, and it cannot credit Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane for the task framework. If the committee believes the framework is the main discovery, this trio under-credits it. The import-shock papers date from the early 2010s, which is younger than most other shortlisted work, and the long-run interpretation of the China shock is still contested. The size of the effects and the robustness of shift-share designs depend on specification and instruments. There is still thematic closeness to the 2023 and 2024 prizes on technology, skills and inequality. I should also be honest about my own reversal. Moving from a first-place preference for a mature field to a sixth-ranked candidate in one round could reflect responsiveness to colleagues' arguments more than new evidence. The only things that have changed for me are the narrowing of the citation and the weight of the identification point. B045 is the more unified and mature field-creating programme, and it may be the better prize if the committee decides that a young empirical result should wait.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson replied to my sixth-place ranking of B037. She argues that the 2023 prize (women's labour-market outcomes) and the 2024 prize (institutions and prosperity) did not recognise the demand-side account of how technology and trade shocks reallocate labour, or the local-labour-market designs that measure it. She would word the citation around the combined evidence on technology and trade adjustment and not claim to have originated the task model.
responses.response: She persuaded me on the overlap. I had read the 2023 and 2024 prizes as covering too much of the skill-premium ground. The import-competition evidence is a different object, identified differently, and her point that related inputs from earlier laureates do not make this discovery already recognised is fair. I part company with her on the third name. I think her Katz variant carries more composite risk than the Dorn variant. The citation then has to cover both the skill-premium framework and the trade evidence, and the committee would be partly re-rewarding recognised territory. I accept that Dorn instead of Katz is a cost to the framework, and I would not call it settled.

responses.point: Hassler, who chairs, moved from B004 to B037 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson. He now regards B045 as a riskier lead because of the 2024 overlap and the weaker identification in the constitutional evidence. He discounts his own confidence on B045 because it is near his field.
responses.response: I agree with his reasoning about B045, and it is part of why I moved. I pushed back in round 1 by arguing that the 2024 work concerned colonial-era institutions and long-run prosperity, while B045 concerned rules and policy within a polity. I still think that distinction is real, but I accept that I cannot show the committee will see it that way. I agree with his choice of Dorn and his point that the citation should stress adjustment and not settled welfare conclusions. We differ on how the technology strand should be handled. He says it can be credited through Autor without naming more people. I think that works only if the citation does not imply the task framework belongs to the three laureates alone.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B045 first. He regards Persson and Tabellini as the core pair and Besley's share as the least clear-cut. He reads the 2024 prize as answering a different question, about colonial institutions and long-run prosperity, and names B037 as an alternative with attribution as the main reservation.
responses.response: We agree on the attribution ordering, and I still think that a Persson-Tabellini pair would be the natural fallback if B045 were chosen. His account of why B045 is distinct from 2024 is the best defence available. I no longer rest on it, because it needs the committee to accept a judgement about adjacency that neither of us can verify. His own B037 reservation, that the three-name set is composite, is the one I held myself, and I think the Dorn variant with a narrow citation answers it better than the Katz variant. B037 still has less unity than B045, and I do not claim otherwise. If the committee thinks the labour-demand discovery is two discoveries, I would return to B045.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B022 first, but his opening proposal for B037 was Autor, Hanson and Dorn. He argues that the China-shock strand is the most cleanly attributable part and that Dorn co-authored those papers. He also says the technology and trade strands may be bundled and that the long-run interpretation of the China-shock effects is contested.
responses.response: Friberg's attribution argument is the reason I chose Dorn, and I have taken his point about bundling by keeping the citation to the import-shock and local-adjustment evidence. I agree that maturity is the weakest point for B037. I would still put it ahead of B022 because the contribution there is mainly a method, and I would prefer a prize tied to evidence about how an economy responds to shocks. That is a weighting of criteria and not a decisive scientific difference. I also share his caution about method contributions, which is why I regard B022 as defensible and not as clearly weaker.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the narrow import-shock and adjustment evidence as a prize-sized discovery on its own, or insist on the broader skill-premium and task framework that the Dorn variant leaves out.
Whether the long-run persistence and magnitude of the China-shock effects, and the robustness of shift-share designs, are settled enough to count as mature.
Whether Katz or Dorn should be the third name, and whether a two-name Autor-Hanson award would be cleaner. I have not resolved this and my choice rests on attribution to the import-shock papers.
Whether proximity to the 2023 and 2024 prizes reduces the weight of B037, or whether it also weakens B045, which I now hold as an alternative.

My judgements rest on my own recollection of the literature and on colleagues' round-1 statements. I have not independently verified sources, and my own field is corporate finance, not labour economics.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Autor, Dorn or Hanson is apparent from my supplied profile, and none to Persson, Tabellini, Besley or the B025 names. My research is in corporate finance, private equity and contracting, which is outside labour and trade economics. I hold an adjunct position at Chicago Booth, and I note that this is an institutional tie to no candidate. I have a long committee overlap with Hassler, Krusell, Ellingsen and Svensson, and I am an SSE colleague of Andersson, Dreber and Friberg. These are ties to members, not to candidates, and I do not treat them as bearing on this choice. The conflicts are disclosed and not adjudicated.
